shortQuestions: Reactive adhesives harden by a chemical reaction (polymerisation or cross-linking) after application, e.g. two-part epoxy, polyurethane, cyanoacrylate (super glue, cured by moisture); the bond is strong and resistant to heat and solvents.

Non-reactive adhesives harden by a physical change — evaporation of solvent or water (white PVA glue, rubber cement), cooling of a melt (hot-melt glue) or simple pressure (pressure-sensitive tapes); no chemical reaction occurs.
Nail polish is a film of nitrocellulose and resins with plasticisers and pigments, left behind when its solvent evaporates.
The remover (acetone or ethyl acetate) is a strong solvent that dissolves these film-forming polymers again, so the film softens and can be wiped off with cotton.
Temporary hair dyes contain large dye molecules (or pigments) that only coat the outer surface (cuticle) of the hair; they cannot enter the hair shaft, and there is no chemical bonding with the hair.
So they are held weakly and are washed out by a single shampoo.

Petrochemicals (primary or base petrochemicals) are the basic chemicals obtained directly from petroleum and natural gas by refining and cracking: ethylene, propylene, butadiene, benzene, toluene, xylene, methanol, synthesis gas.

Chemicals derived from them are the end products made by further reactions of these base chemicals: plastics (polythene, PVC, polystyrene), synthetic fibres (nylon, polyester), synthetic rubber, detergents, solvents, paints, fertilisers, pesticides and drugs.

Addition polymers are formed when unsaturated monomers (C=C) add to one another without losing any atoms; the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer, e.g. polythene, PVC, polystyrene (chain-growth).

Condensation polymers are formed when monomers with two functional groups join with the loss of a small molecule such as H₂O or HCl; the repeat unit differs from the monomers, e.g. nylon-6,6, polyesters (terylene), bakelite (step-growth).

Acetone is a very strong solvent: it removes the natural oils of nails and skin, leaving them dry, brittle and cracked; it has a strong smell, is highly flammable and can damage artificial nails and some surfaces.

Non-acetone removers (based on ethyl acetate, propylene carbonate, etc.) are gentler and less drying, so they are better for regular use and for artificial nails — although they work more slowly on dark or glitter polish.

Chemical and process industries handle toxic, flammable, explosive and corrosive substances, often at high temperatures and pressures; accidents (fires, explosions, gas leaks such as Bhopal) can kill or injure workers and nearby people and damage the environment.

Safety measures — training, protective equipment, ventilation, safe design, maintenance, emergency plans — protect workers' lives and health, prevent loss of property and production, and are required by law. A safe workplace also improves morale and productivity.
The main goal of petroleum refining is to separate crude oil into useful fractions (by fractional distillation) and convert them (by cracking, reforming and other processes) into high-value products.
These are fuels (LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil), lubricants, wax and bitumen, and feedstock for petrochemicals; impurities such as sulphur are also removed.
longQuestions: (a) Petrochemical process technology converts petroleum and natural gas into basic chemicals and then into finished products. Steps: (i) refining — crude oil is desalted and separated by fractional distillation into fractions such as naphtha and gas oil; (ii) conversion — steam cracking of ethane or naphtha gives olefins (ethylene, propylene, butadiene); catalytic reforming of naphtha gives aromatics (benzene, toluene, xylenes — BTX); steam reforming of natural gas gives synthesis gas (CO + H₂) for methanol and ammonia; (iii) further processes — polymerisation, oxidation, alkylation, chlorination, etc. — turn these into plastics, fibres, rubber, detergents, solvents and fertilisers.
(b) Cracking breaks large, less useful hydrocarbons into smaller ones (petrol-range alkanes and alkenes), e.g. C₁₆H₃₄ → C₈H₁₈ + C₈H₁₆.
Thermal cracking: heating at about 450–750 °C under pressure without catalyst; free-radical mechanism; gives many alkenes.

Catalytic cracking: about 450–550 °C at low pressure over zeolite or silica–alumina catalysts (fluid catalytic cracking); carbocation mechanism; gives branched alkanes and aromatics — high-octane petrol.

Steam cracking: hydrocarbons mixed with steam heated to about 850 °C for a very short time; main source of ethylene and propylene. Hydrocracking: cracking with hydrogen under high pressure over a catalyst; gives saturated products such as diesel and jet fuel, and removes sulphur.

(a) Lipstick consists of waxes (beeswax, carnauba, candelilla) for shape and firmness, oils (castor oil, mineral oil, lanolin) for gloss and easy spreading, emollients, pigments and dyes (iron oxides, titanium dioxide, eosin/bromo acids, lakes) for colour, plus antioxidants, preservatives, perfume and flavour.

Preparation: the waxes and oils are melted together (about 80 °C); the pigments are ground finely in part of the oil (roller mill) and blended into the melt; perfume is added; the hot mixture is poured into metal moulds and cooled; the sticks are removed, passed briefly through a flame to give a glossy surface, and fixed in their cases.
Applications: colouring and beautifying the lips, moisturising and protecting them from drying and cracking; some contain sunscreens (SPF) or medicinal agents (lip balms).

(b) Nail polish composition: film former — nitrocellulose (forms a hard, glossy film); resins — e.g. tosylamide–formaldehyde resin for adhesion and gloss; plasticisers — camphor, dibutyl phthalate or citrates for flexibility; solvents — ethyl acetate, butyl acetate, isopropyl alcohol (dissolve the components and evaporate quickly); pigments — iron oxides, titanium dioxide, mica or guanine for pearl effects; thickening/suspending agents (stearalkonium hectorite) and UV stabilisers.
(a) Adhesives are substances that hold two surfaces together by adhesion (attraction to the surfaces) and cohesion (internal strength).

By origin: natural adhesives — from animals or plants: animal glue (bones, hides), casein glue (milk), starch and dextrin pastes, natural rubber; synthetic adhesives — epoxies, polyvinyl acetate (white glue), polyurethanes, cyanoacrylates, polyimides, acrylics.

By reactiveness: non-reactive adhesives harden physically — drying (solvent/water based), contact, hot-melt and pressure-sensitive adhesives; reactive adhesives harden chemically — one-part (cyanoacrylates, moisture- or heat-cured) and multi-part (two-part epoxies, polyurethanes) that react when mixed.

(b) Importance: furniture and woodwork (plywood, laminates); building and construction (tiles, panels, sealants); packaging (cartons, labels, envelopes, tapes); automobile and aircraft manufacture (light, strong joints instead of rivets); electronics; shoes and leather goods; bookbinding and stationery; medicine (bandages, surgical glues, dentures); and everyday household repairs.

(a) Raw materials in Pakistan: natural gas (Sui and other fields) — fertilisers (ammonia, urea), methanol, power; crude oil (Potwar region, Sindh) — refineries and petrochemicals; coal (Thar, Lakhra, Salt Range) — power and coke; rock salt (Khewra) — caustic soda, chlorine, soda ash; limestone, clay and gypsum — cement and lime; rock phosphate (Hazara) — phosphatic fertilisers; sulphur — sulphuric acid; sugarcane and molasses — sugar and ethanol; cotton — textiles; wood, bagasse and wheat straw — paper; chromite, iron ore and other minerals — metallurgical and chemical industries.

(b) Safety considerations in process industries: (i) hazard identification and risk assessment of chemicals, temperatures and pressures; (ii) safe plant design with relief valves, interlocks, alarms and automatic shut-down; (iii) safe storage and handling of flammable, toxic and corrosive materials with proper labelling and Material Safety Data Sheets; (iv) personal protective equipment — goggles, gloves, helmets, masks, safety shoes; (v) fire prevention, detectors and fire-fighting equipment; (vi) ventilation and gas monitoring; (vii) training, safe work procedures and permits; (viii) regular inspection and maintenance; (ix) emergency plans, drills, first aid and medical care; (x) proper waste treatment and pollution control, following national safety and environmental laws.

(a) Fractional distillation of petroleum: crude oil is heated in a furnace to about 400 °C and the vapour enters the bottom of a tall fractionating column, which is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. Vapours rise through trays; each component condenses at the level where the temperature equals its boiling point and is drawn off.

Fractions (from top to bottom): refinery gas (C₁–C₄; LPG, fuel and feedstock); petrol/gasoline (C₅–C₁₀; motor fuel); naphtha (C₆–C₁₀; petrochemical feedstock); kerosene (C₁₀–C₁₆; jet fuel, lamps, stoves); diesel/gas oil (C₁₄–C₂₀; diesel engines); lubricating oil (C₂₀–C₃₀); fuel oil (ships, power stations); paraffin wax; residue — bitumen/asphalt (roads, roofing).

(b) Importance of chemical industries to Pakistan's economy: fertilisers raise agricultural production and food security; cement supports construction and infrastructure; textile chemicals and dyes serve the largest export sector; pharmaceuticals, soaps, detergents, paints, plastics, paper, glass, sugar and ethanol meet daily needs.

They provide employment to many people, use local raw materials (gas, salt, limestone, coal), reduce imports and save foreign exchange, earn export income, pay taxes and contribute significantly to GDP and industrial growth.
activities: Sample newspaper article — 'Petrochemicals: the hidden ingredients of modern life'. Crude oil and natural gas are not only fuels; they are the starting point of thousands of everyday products. After crude oil is refined into fractions, parts such as naphtha and natural gas are cracked and reformed into basic petrochemicals — ethylene, propylene, butadiene, benzene, toluene, xylene and methanol. These are turned into plastics, synthetic fibres, rubber, detergents, fertilisers, medicines and paints. From the shirt we wear to the phone we hold, petrochemicals are everywhere — which is why using them wisely and recycling plastics is so important. (The article answers the questions below.)
Petroleum was formed from the remains of tiny marine plants and animals (plankton) that died millions of years ago and were buried in mud and sand on the sea floor.

Under high temperature and pressure, without oxygen, this organic matter slowly changed into hydrocarbons, which moved into porous rocks (sandstone, limestone) and were trapped beneath impervious rock layers, forming oil and gas reservoirs.
Crude oil is first desalted and then heated to about 400 °C and separated by fractional distillation in a tall column into fractions according to boiling point.

Fractions: refinery gas (LPG), petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, fuel oil, paraffin wax and bitumen. Heavy fractions are then cracked and reformed to give more petrol and alkenes, and impurities such as sulphur are removed.

Petrochemicals are produced mainly by: steam cracking of ethane, propane or naphtha, giving ethylene, propylene and butadiene; catalytic reforming of naphtha, giving benzene, toluene and xylenes; steam reforming of natural gas, giving synthesis gas (CO + H₂) for methanol and ammonia.
These basic chemicals are then polymerised, oxidised, chlorinated, etc. to make plastics, fibres and other chemicals.

Famous petrochemicals: ethylene, propylene, butadiene, benzene, toluene, xylene, methanol, styrene, vinyl chloride, ethylene oxide/ethylene glycol and acetone; and products from them such as polythene, PVC, polystyrene, nylon, polyester and synthetic rubber.

Petrochemicals serve as raw materials for plastics and packaging, synthetic fibres and textiles, synthetic rubber and tyres, detergents and soaps, solvents, paints and adhesives, fertilisers and pesticides, medicines and cosmetics, explosives and dyes.
Almost every modern product contains petrochemicals — clothing, packaging, medical equipment, car parts, electronics, building materials and household goods — so modern life depends on them.

They create jobs and industries and support agriculture (fertilisers) and health (medicines). At the same time they come from non-renewable resources and plastics cause pollution, so they must be used responsibly and recycled.
